title: How does a service registry like Netflix Eureka work — each service instance registers itself on startup (heartbeat-based lease), clients query the registry to discover available instances, and stale registrations are evicted after missed heartbeats — and how does Kubernetes-native service discovery (CoreDNS + Service objects) differ from Eureka (no separate registry server, the platform handles it), and when do you still need Eureka (non-Kubernetes environments, multi-cloud, gradual migration)?
shortTitle: How does a service registry like Netflix Eureka work, and how does Kubernetes-native discovery differ?

s1_definition.profdef: A service registry is a central directory of which service instances are currently running and reachable. With Netflix Eureka, each instance registers itself with the Eureka server on startup, declaring its service name and network address, and then renews a time-bounded lease by sending periodic heartbeats; if heartbeats stop arriving, the lease expires and Eureka evicts the stale registration. Clients query Eureka to get the current list of healthy instances for a service and then load-balance across them client-side. Kubernetes-native discovery achieves the same outcome without a separate registry application: you declare a Service object, the platform tracks which pods are healthy via readiness probes and endpoint controllers, and CoreDNS resolves the service name to those endpoints, so discovery is a built-in platform capability rather than a library plus a server you operate. You still reach for Eureka when you are not on Kubernetes, when you span multiple clouds or mixed environments where no single platform owns discovery, or during a gradual migration where some services are on Kubernetes and others are not.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has many branches that open and close through the day, and customers need to know which branches are currently open to serve them. Eureka is like a central phone directory the bank keeps: every branch phones in when it opens and keeps calling every thirty seconds to say "still open"; if a branch stops calling, the directory crosses it off. A customer rings the directory, gets the list of open branches, and picks one. Kubernetes-native discovery is like the bank building having a smart reception desk built into the walls: you do not run a separate directory office, because the building itself knows which rooms are staffed and, when you ask for "the loans department," it points you to a currently-staffed loans room automatically. You would still keep the old phone directory if your branches are spread across several different buildings run by different companies, where no single smart building knows about all of them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Eureka is a self-registration directory with heartbeat leases and client-side lookup; Kubernetes bakes the same thing into the platform via Services and CoreDNS, and Eureka remains useful off-Kubernetes, across clouds, or mid-migration.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A service registry is a central directory of which service instances are currently running and reachable. With Netflix Eureka, each instance registers itself with the Eureka server on startup, declaring its service name and network address, and then renews a time-bounded lease by sending periodic heartbeats; if heartbeats stop arriving, the lease expires and Eureka evicts the stale registration. You still reach for Eureka when you are not on Kubernetes, when you span multiple clouds or mixed environments where no single platform owns discovery, or during a gradual migration where some services are on Kubernetes and others are not.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has many branches that open and close through the day, and customers need to know which branches are currently open to serve them. Eureka is like a central phone directory the bank keeps: every branch phones in when it opens and keeps calling every thirty seconds to say "still open"; if a branch stops calling, the directory crosses it off. A customer rings the directory, gets the list of open branches, and picks one. Kubernetes-native discovery is like the bank building having a smart reception desk built into the walls: you do not run a separate directory office, because the building itself knows which rooms are staffed and, when you ask for "the loans department," it points you to a currently-staffed loans room automatically. sections.s2_technical:
In a microservices system, instances come and go constantly — they scale up, scale down, crash, restart, and move hosts — so no caller can hardcode addresses. Service discovery is the mechanism that answers "where are the healthy instances of service X right now." There are two broad styles, and Eureka and Kubernetes represent them.

Eureka implements client-side discovery with a dedicated registry server. The lifecycle has three parts. On startup, each instance registers with Eureka, sending its service name, host, port, and metadata. This creates a lease. To keep the lease alive, the instance sends a heartbeat on a fixed interval, by default every thirty seconds; each heartbeat renews the lease. If Eureka does not receive heartbeats within the lease-expiration window, it evicts that instance from the registry, so stale or dead instances fall out automatically. On the client side, callers fetch the registry — typically caching it locally and refreshing periodically — and then pick an instance using a client-side load balancer. The client, not a central proxy, decides which instance to call.

```java
// Eureka client-side discovery (conceptual): fetch instances, load-balance locally
List<InstanceInfo> instances = eurekaClient.getInstancesByServiceName("transfer-service");
InstanceInfo chosen = clientLoadBalancer.choose(instances); // client decides
String url = "http://" + chosen.getIPAddr() + ":" + chosen.getPort() + "/api/v1/transfers";
```

A notable property of Eureka is that it deliberately favours availability over strict consistency. During a network partition it enters self-preservation mode, keeping registrations it can no longer confirm rather than evicting everything, on the theory that stale-but-maybe-alive entries are safer than an empty registry that makes the whole system undiscoverable. This is an AP choice in CAP terms, appropriate for discovery where a temporarily stale list is better than no list.

Kubernetes-native discovery removes the separate registry application by making discovery a platform responsibility. You declare a Service object that selects a set of pods by label. The platform's endpoint controller continuously tracks which of those pods are ready — using readiness probes — and maintains the Service's endpoint list. CoreDNS, the in-cluster DNS server, resolves the Service's name (for example transfer-service.default.svc.cluster.local) to the Service's stable virtual IP or directly to the ready pod endpoints. A caller simply makes an HTTP request to the service name, DNS resolves it, and kube-proxy or the Service load-balances to a healthy pod. There is no registration library in the application and no heartbeat you write; the application just exposes a readiness endpoint, and the platform does registration, health tracking, eviction, and load balancing.

```yaml
# Kubernetes: the Service IS the discovery mechanism — no Eureka server, no client library
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: transfer-service }
spec:
  selector: { app: transfer }     # platform tracks ready pods with this label
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
# Caller just does: http://transfer-service/api/v1/transfers  (CoreDNS resolves it)
```

The key differences follow from this. Eureka requires you to run and operate a registry cluster and embed a client library in every service, giving you client-side load balancing and rich metadata, and it works anywhere there is a network. Kubernetes-native discovery requires no extra server or library because the platform owns it, uses DNS plus readiness probes rather than application heartbeats, and typically does server-side or kube-proxy load balancing, but it only works within the Kubernetes world. So the senior-level guidance on when you still need Eureka: when your services are not on Kubernetes at all, for example on virtual machines or bare metal; when you span multiple clouds or hybrid on-premise-plus-cloud environments where no single Kubernetes cluster owns every instance; and during a gradual migration where some services already run on Kubernetes while others do not, and you need one discovery mechanism that spans both until the migration completes. In a greenfield, single-cluster Kubernetes deployment, adding Eureka is usually redundant complexity because the platform already provides discovery; the honest principal-level answer is to use the platform's native mechanism when you are fully on the platform, and reach for an explicit registry like Eureka precisely when you are not, or not yet.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the transfer service needs to call the account service, whose instances scale up and down and occasionally crash. Callers cannot hardcode addresses.

Problem 1 — without discovery, a crashed account instance still receives traffic and transfers fail. The system needs a live directory of healthy instances with automatic eviction of dead ones.

Problem 2 — the bank is partway through moving to Kubernetes: some services are already in a cluster using Services and CoreDNS, while older services still run on virtual machines and need an explicit registry. The design must handle both.

The mini-project simulates a Eureka-style registry with registration, heartbeat leases, and eviction after missed heartbeats, plus client-side lookup and load balancing, and contrasts it with a Kubernetes-style discovery that resolves a service name to ready endpoints with no application heartbeat. The demo registers account instances, shows a client discovering and load-balancing across them, crashes one instance so its lease expires and it is evicted, and then shows the Kubernetes-style resolver returning only ready endpoints without any heartbeat logic in the application.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: two account-service instances register with a Eureka-style registry, a client discovers and load-balances across them, one instance crashes, and then a Kubernetes-style resolver returns ready endpoints.

Step 1 — Instances register. On startup, acct-1 and acct-2 register with the registry, each declaring its service name and address. Each registration creates a lease stamped with the current time. The registry now knows two healthy account instances.

Step 2 — Client discovers and load-balances. The client asks the registry for healthy account-service instances, gets both, and the client-side load balancer picks acct-1 for the first call and acct-2 for the second, round-robin. The client, not a central proxy, chooses the instance.

Step 3 — One instance crashes. acct-1 crashes and stops sending heartbeats. Time advances past the lease-expiration window. acct-2, still alive, sends a heartbeat that renews its lease.

Step 4 — Eviction. The registry runs eviction and finds that acct-1's last heartbeat is older than the lease window, so it evicts acct-1. Now only acct-2 remains healthy. The next client lookup returns just acct-2, so no traffic is sent to the dead instance. The heartbeat lease mechanism removed the dead instance automatically.

Step 5 — Kubernetes-native resolution. For the services already on Kubernetes, there is no registry server and no application heartbeat. The platform's endpoint controller tracks which pods are ready via readiness probes, and CoreDNS resolves the service name account-service to the current ready endpoints. The caller simply makes a request to the name and the platform routes it to a healthy pod. The same outcome — discover healthy instances — is achieved, but the application wrote no registration or heartbeat code at all.

```
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] === Eureka-style discovery ===
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] REGISTER acct-1 (account-service @ 10.0.0.1:8080)
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] REGISTER acct-2 (account-service @ 10.0.0.2:8080)
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] Client chose acct-1 @ 10.0.0.1:8080
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] Client chose acct-2 @ 10.0.0.2:8080
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [WARNING] EVICT acct-1 (lease expired)
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] Healthy account instances now = 1
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] Client chose acct-2 @ 10.0.0.2:8080
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] === Kubernetes-native discovery (no registry server, no heartbeat) ===
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] CoreDNS resolve account-service → 2 ready endpoint(s)
2026-10-24 19:40:15 [INFO] Caller uses http://account-service — platform routes to [10.1.0.5:8080, 10.1.0.6:8080]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A service registry exists because in a microservices system instances come and go constantly — they scale, crash, restart, and move — so no caller can hardcode addresses, and something has to answer "where are the healthy instances of this service right now." Netflix Eureka answers it with client-side discovery backed by a dedicated registry server. The lifecycle has three parts: on startup each instance registers with Eureka, sending its service name and address, which creates a lease; the instance keeps that lease alive by sending a heartbeat on a fixed interval, by default every thirty seconds; and if Eureka stops receiving heartbeats within the lease window, it evicts the instance, so dead or stale instances fall out automatically. On the client side, callers fetch the registry, cache it, and use a client-side load balancer to pick an instance themselves, so the caller, not a central proxy, decides where the request goes. A characteristic detail is that Eureka favours availability over consistency — during a network partition it enters self-preservation and keeps registrations it cannot confirm, because a stale list is safer for discovery than an empty one.

Kubernetes-native discovery reaches the same outcome but removes the separate registry application by making discovery a platform responsibility. You declare a Service object that selects pods by label, the platform's endpoint controller continuously tracks which of those pods are ready using readiness probes, and CoreDNS, the in-cluster DNS server, resolves the service name to those ready endpoints. A caller just makes an HTTP request to the service name, DNS resolves it, and kube-proxy load-balances to a healthy pod. The crucial difference is that the application writes no registration and no heartbeat code; it only exposes a readiness endpoint, and the platform handles registration, health tracking, eviction, and load balancing. Eureka is a library plus a server you operate with application heartbeats and client-side load balancing; Kubernetes is a built-in capability using DNS and probes with platform-side load balancing.

So the honest answer to when you still need Eureka is that it depends on whether a single platform owns all your instances. If you are fully on a single Kubernetes cluster, adding Eureka is usually redundant complexity, because the platform already provides discovery natively. You still want an explicit registry like Eureka when your services are not on Kubernetes at all — on virtual machines or bare metal — when you span multiple clouds or a hybrid on-premise-plus-cloud estate where no single cluster knows about every instance, and during a gradual migration where some services already run on Kubernetes and others do not, and you need one discovery mechanism that spans both worlds until the migration finishes.

In my banking work this mapped directly onto a migration: older account and transfer services ran on virtual machines and used a Eureka registry with heartbeat leases and client-side load balancing, while newer services ran in a Kubernetes cluster and used Services plus CoreDNS with no discovery code in the application at all. During the transition we kept Eureka as the bridge so both worlds could discover each other, and we retired it for a given service only once that service was fully inside the cluster. The principle I take into interviews is that service discovery is the same problem everywhere — find the healthy instances and route to them — and the right tool is whatever already owns your runtime: the platform's native mechanism when you are on the platform, and an explicit registry like Eureka precisely when you are not, not yet, or spread across several.
